name: manual_0c524b
claim:
Prior art from a real supersession-scope incident on lesson_757476abb44e/lesson_fad3af10b7cd -- five distinct, reusable golden nuggets for any future agent working with this memory system's supersession mechanism, or any similar "record X replaces record Y" architecture elsewhere.

(1) THE ARCHITECTURAL RISK, generalizable beyond this repo: any system where superseding one record excludes it WHOLESALE from active retrieval -- rather than comparing what specific content the successor actually covers -- can silently destroy correct, still-valid information the moment a NARROW correction supersedes a BROADER multi-topic record. Concretely here: lesson_757476abb44e held four distinct claims (watcher deadlock, hand-waving diagnostic method, PR-locality/non-merge discipline, authorization evidence). lesson_fad3af10b7cd correctly refined ONLY the authorization claim, but marking it as the formal supersessor caused recall._load_structured() to drop ALL FOUR claims from structured recall, not just the one being corrected -- confirmed by reading `if lid in retired: continue` in .agent/tools/recall.py directly, which happens with zero content-scope comparison. GENERAL RULE: before marking any multi-topic record as superseded by a narrower successor, first verify (by reading the successor's actual claim text, not assuming) whether it covers the FULL scope of what's being retired. If it doesn't, extract and separately preserve the uncovered content as its own accepted record BEFORE relying on the supersession -- do this in the same change, not as a follow-up, since a gap here silently deletes correct guidance with no error, no warning, and no indication anything is wrong until someone goes looking for content that's mysteriously gone.

(2) A SPECIFIC, NON-OBVIOUS TECHNICAL TRAP in this exact codebase: render_lessons.py's superseded_by_map() only treats rows with status=="accepted" as valid superseders -- `if L.get("status") != "accepted": continue` runs BEFORE the supersedes field is even read. This means setting a `supersedes` field on a row with status="legacy" (or "provisional", or anything else) has ZERO rendering/exclusion effect -- confirmed by testing the wrong direction first and catching it before committing, not by reading the source alone. If you need to retire a non-"accepted" row (e.g. an auto-migrated status="legacy" duplicate from render_lessons.py's stray-bullet migration pass), the fix runs in the OPPOSITE direction from what's intuitive: create or reuse an ACCEPTED record whose own `supersedes` field points AT the row you want retired, not the reverse.

(3) VERIFY BY EXECUTION, not by reading code and reasoning about what it should do: after patching lessons.jsonl directly (a case where a hand-edit was appropriate -- fixing a structured field on an existing, not-yet-externally-built-upon record, matching this repo's own established exception), the fix was confirmed by actually importing and calling recall._load_structured() directly in a Python one-liner and checking the real output list, not by re-reading the JSONL and asserting it "should" work. This caught nothing wrong here, but the discipline is the point: for any fix to retrieval/rendering logic, run the actual consuming function against the actual current file state before considering the fix complete.

(4) CHECK REVIEW TIMING BEFORE ASSUMING A CONTRADICTION IS REAL: a review comment appeared to directly contradict a fix already verified and pushed minutes earlier. Rather than assume either the review or the prior verification was wrong, checked the review object's own `commit_id` field via the GitHub API against the actual current branch tip -- confirmed the review was posted against an older commit, one push behind. This resolved the apparent contradiction cleanly and is a reusable check for any "this review says X is broken but I just verified X is fixed" situation: compare timestamps/commit SHAs directly rather than guessing which side is stale.

(5) WHEN A SINGLE HAND-EDIT ISN'T ENOUGH, CHECK WHETHER IT NEEDS A COMPANION FIX: fixing the primary finding (the scope-mismatched supersession) surfaced a second, related-but-distinct bug during investigation that neither review comment had named directly -- a stray, auto-migrated, zero-evidence duplicate lesson (status="legacy") that would have kept rendering confusingly regardless of how the primary fix was implemented. Found by reading render_lessons.py's migration logic (`rationale: "Imported from pre-restructure LESSONS.md bullets below sentinel"`) to understand WHY a near-duplicate existed at all, rather than treating it as an unexplained oddity to route around. General habit: when a fix touches a system with automated derivation/migration logic, understand that logic's actual mechanism before concluding an anomaly is unrelated noise.

decisions.notes: Direct request to preserve this investigation's reusable insights as prior art for future agents -- five distinct, verified techniques and gotchas from a real supersession-scope incident.
